fixes.explanation: Nice try, but the text doesn't say Paul is admiring any artwork. It says he was “…deeply disturbed in his spirit to see that the city was full of idols.” Disturbed is the word the text gives us. That's the answer.

Paul isn't described as sightseeing. The text says he was “…deeply disturbed in his spirit…” to see that the city was full of idols. I think a man who's that stirred up has something on his heart. That's the answer.

Right, it's false. Paul doesn't keep quiet in Athens. He reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and God-fearing Gentiles. He also reasoned in the marketplace with those he met each day. I think Silas and Timothy had no idea what they'd find when they got there!

That's it. Besides the synagogue, Paul reasoned “…in the marketplace with those he met each day.” So his talking wasn't limited to one building. Every day he's out there, meeting people and reasoning with them.

The text doesn't mention a city gate here. It says Paul reasoned in the synagogue, and in the marketplace with those he met each day. I know a gate sounds official, but the marketplace is the answer. It's the other place he talks with people daily.

No riverside in this passage, friend. The text says Paul reasoned in the synagogue, and in the marketplace with those he met each day. I bet a quiet spot by the water sounds nice. But the marketplace is the answer.

Yes. The text says they said this “…because Paul was proclaiming the good news of Jesus and the resurrection.” Some of them said he seemed to be advocating foreign gods. That's the reason the text gives.

Nothing in the text says Paul is speaking in a language they don't know. They even ask him what his new teaching is and say they want to know what it means. The writer tells us the reason for their remark: Paul was proclaiming the good news of Jesus and the resurrection. That's the answer.

That's the one. The writer says they spent their time “…doing nothing more than hearing and articulating new ideas.” Talking and listening, that's their whole schedule. If you ask me, that's a lot of ideas and a lot of ears.

Not what Paul says. He says the God who made the world is the Lord of heaven and earth and “…does not live in temples made by human hands.” So the answer is False. The temples in Athens aren't where this God lives.

Right, it's false. Paul says the God who made the world is the Lord of heaven and earth and “…does not live in temples made by human hands.” I think that would've been a surprise to a city full of temples. And Paul says it right there in front of them.

Rest sounds nice, but that's not the command. Paul says God “…now commands all people everywhere to repent.” To repent is to turn around and change direction. And the command goes to all people everywhere, not just the folks in front of Paul.

That's not what Paul says here. He says God has set a day when He “…will judge the world with justice by the Man He has appointed.” Judging the world with justice is the answer, and wars don't come up in this speech. I know it's a big thing to say to a crowd, but Paul says it plain.
Right on. Paul says God “…has given proof of this to everyone by raising Him from the dead.” The proof is something God did. He raised the Man He appointed.
Paul doesn't mention any signs in the sky. He says God “…has given proof of this to everyone by raising Him from the dead.” The proof is the raising from the dead. That's the answer.
That's it. When they heard about the resurrection of the dead, “…some began to mock him…” The text says some, not everyone. And right after that, we hear from others who respond differently.
Actually it's true. Alongside the ones who mock, others said, “We want to hear you again on this topic.” So they're not finished with the conversation. The same speech gets two different reactions.

Yes, Damaris. The text says some joined Paul and believed, including Dionysius the Areopagite, “…a woman named Damaris, and others who were with them.” Dionysius, a member of the Areopagus, is named, and so is she. I think that's worth remembering.
